questions.question: Describe the two British colonies in southern Africa around 1860, including how and when each came under British rule and one feature of how each was governed.
questions.expected_answer: The Cape Colony: settled by the Dutch East India Company from 1652, taken by Britain in 1795 and permanently in 1806 to protect the sea route to India; slavery ended in 1834; it received representative government in 1853 with a non-racial franchise based on property worth 25 pounds or a certain income, though most voters were white; it fought frontier wars with Xhosa chiefdoms and annexed British Kaffraria in 1847. Natal: British traders at Port Natal from 1824; Voortrekkers set up the Republic of Natalia after 1838; Britain annexed it in 1843 and it became a separate colony in 1856; Shepstone settled Africans in locations governed through chiefs under customary law; sugar was grown on the coast from the 1850s.

questions.question: Explain why the Voortrekkers left the Cape and how the two Boer republics gained recognition.
questions.expected_answer: Reasons: dissatisfaction with British rule; the end of slavery in 1834 and compensation they considered unfair; Ordinance 50 of 1828 giving Khoekhoe and free people of colour legal equality; shortage of land; insecurity on the eastern frontier; a desire to govern themselves and control land and labour. Britain at first annexed the land between the Orange and Vaal as the Orange River Sovereignty in 1848 but found it costly and withdrew. The Sand River Convention of 1852 recognised the South African Republic north of the Vaal, and the Bloemfontein Convention of 1854 recognised the Orange Free State between the Orange and Vaal. Both restricted arms sales to Africans and reserved citizenship for white men.

questions.question: Name four independent African kingdoms or chiefdoms on the map of southern Africa around 1860, their rulers or locations, and explain one example of conflict or diplomacy.
questions.expected_answer: Any four: the Zulu kingdom between the Thukela and Phongolo under Mpande with Cetshwayo rising; the Swazi kingdom under Mswati II; the Basotho under Moshoeshoe at Thaba Bosiu; the Pedi under Sekwati and Sekhukhune; Tswana chiefdoms such as the Ngwato and Kwena; Xhosa chiefdoms east of the Kei; the Mpondo; the Venda; the Gaza kingdom of Soshangane; the Griqua under Waterboer and Adam Kok III. Example: Moshoeshoe used diplomacy and war to defend Basotho land west of the Caledon against the Orange Free State and in 1868 asked for British protection, which preserved Lesotho as a separate state.
